LISBON - City officials announced on Tuesday that the long awaited renovation of the riverside tram line will begin early next spring, bringing to an end nearly a decade of debate over how to modernize one of the oldest public transport routes in Europe. The project, which carries an estimated budget of ninety million euros, will replace worn tracks, upgrade stations and introduce quieter, lower floor vehicles designed to improve access for passengers with limited mobility.

Residents of the historic neighborhoods along the route have expressed mixed feelings. Some shopkeepers worry that months of construction will keep tourists away during the busiest part of the year, while others argue that a reliable and comfortable tram will bring more visitors in the long run. The mayor promised that temporary shuttle buses would run every ten minutes and that businesses affected by closures would be eligible for tax relief.

Engineers explained that the work will proceed in four phases so that at least half of the line remains open at any time. The first phase covers the steepest hill section, where the old rails have worn unevenly and the brakes of aging cars are under the greatest strain. Crews will also install drainage channels to prevent flooding during heavy autumn rain, a problem that forced several suspensions of service last winter.

Heritage groups secured an important concession in the final plan. Two of the original wooden carriages, painted in the traditional yellow, will be restored and kept in service on weekends as a rolling museum. A small exhibition about the history of the line will open at the central terminus, featuring photographs, tickets and uniforms donated by retired drivers and their families.

Environmental advocates welcomed the decision to power the new fleet with electricity from local solar farms. According to the transport authority, the upgrade should reduce noise by a third and cut annual emissions from replaced diesel buses by several thousand tonnes. Cyclists will gain a protected lane along the river, completing a missing link in the network that connects the airport with the western suburbs.

The city council will vote on the final contract next month, and construction is expected to finish in time for the summer festival two years from now. Officials urged residents to follow the project website for maps, schedules and updates on temporary traffic changes.
